lines: overnight is a Claude Code plugin with a command that runs a piece of work, or a work, that you
give it in Claude Code while you're away, and resumes it by itself after the usage limit or an
error stops it.
overnight is for you when you hand Claude Code work that runs for hours and leave it running at
night. With it, you find the work done by morning, or recorded as failed with its log, without
getting up to type "continue" once the limit lifts.
- overnight doesn't resume a conversation that you have open in Claude Code: it runs work that it
- overnight doesn't run from a terminal outside Claude Code: Claude Code puts the command on the
- overnight doesn't keep your computer awake: before you leave, set the computer not to sleep while
In development, at 0.1.0: what overnight does may still change, and no work has yet run through a
real night on this version.

At the end, you have your tests moved to pytest and committed by morning, from one command that you
typed before you left, though the usage limit stopped the work in the night.
This run shows what overnight aims to do, not a night that someone recorded.

05:03 run 6 done
work 20261128-230012 done after 6 runs
3f9c2a1 Move the tests in tests/unittest_old to pytest
You typed one command. The work went on from where the limit stopped it, 17 minutes after the
limit lifted.
overnight runs your work in Claude Code without you, and each time a run stops short, it waits and
asks Claude to go on in the same conversation, until the work is done or the retries run out.
- macOS or Linux: `uname` shows it.
- Python 3.9 or later, run as `python3`: `python3 --version` shows it.
- Claude Code, logged in: `claude auth status` shows `"loggedIn": true`.
claude plugin marketplace add lovaizu/ccpm
claude plugin install overnight@ccpm
In Claude Code, `! overnight --version` shows `overnight 0.1.0`.

more.good_when: A newcomer sees what a night with overnight gives them (Walkthrough) and why they can trust it (How it works) before the README asks them to check requirements and install, so they decide whether it fits before they set anything up, and meet the install steps when they've decided to start.

A reader who adds up the waits sees why they are enough: How it works says the retries wait 4 hours and 35 minutes in all, and also that the waits span the 5-hour limit, so the reader asks whether a limit that resets more than 4 hours and 35 minutes after the stop leaves the work failed. Once it's good, the reader learns, from how the limit's window and the waits follow from the one way, in which nights the work goes on and in which it ends failed.
A user who wants more than the walkthrough shows, such as every option of the command and its default (whether `--dir` is needed, what `--allowed-tools` takes when left out), knows where to find it.
